claims.text: FeNiCrMn yield strength varies only minimally with strain rate from 77 K to 600 K.

The anomalous strain-rate insensitivity is caused by thermally activated partial-dislocation nucleation against chemical short-range-order and lattice-friction barriers rather than by phase transformation.
The dominant yield mechanism shifts from dislocation nucleation at cryogenic temperatures to lattice-friction-controlled glide at elevated temperatures.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy has an FCC structure.
The initial single crystal is free of precipitates and secondary phases.
Atomic-size or lattice-parameter mismatch among the constituent elements produces substantial lattice friction.
Lattice friction caused by constituent-atom mismatch hinders partial-dislocation motion.
Chemical short-range ordering is an important barrier in FeNiCrMn.
Chemical short-range ordering creates a high Peierls barrier that particularly impedes screw dislocations.
Chemical short-range ordering and lattice friction hinder the nucleation of partial dislocations.
Yield onset is governed by thermally activated dislocation nucleation from free surfaces or pre-existing defects.
The activation volume for yielding is large because dislocations must overcome lattice-friction and short-range-order barriers.
At low temperatures, yielding is an athermal, nucleation-limited process.
At elevated temperatures, thermal fluctuations assist dislocations in overcoming the relevant barriers.
Slip and deformation twinning dominate deformation up to 600 K.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs during initial yielding.
Traditional FCC metals such as pure Ni and Cu have a strong strain-rate dependence governed by dislocation multiplication and drag.
FeNiCrMn alloys can precipitate an additional BCC phase after sufficiently severe high-temperature exposure.
Significant Al additions induce BCC phase stability in related high-entropy alloys.
Yield onset should be anisotropic with respect to the [111] and [100] crystal orientations.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis broadly attributes strain-rate insensitivity to thermally activated nucleation, whereas the mechanism describes the cryogenic nucleation-limited process as athermal.

The hypothesis says the elevated-temperature dominant mechanism becomes lattice-friction-controlled dislocation glide, while the mechanism continues to characterize yield onset as dislocation nucleation from surfaces or pre-existing defects.
